documents.title: HexaNet: Hexagonal Convolutions for Remote-Sensing Scene Classification
pages: HexaNet: Hexagonal Convolutions for Remote-Sensing Scene Classification. SYNTHETIC TEST FIXTURE - fictional content written for software testing; not a real publication. Abstract. We propose HexaNet, a convolutional neural network that replaces square kernels with hexagonal kernels to classify satellite imagery. The objective of this work is to improve scene classification accuracy on aerial images while reducing the number of trainable parameters. Introduction. Remote-sensing scene classification is difficult because aerial images contain rotated objects and repeated textures. Square convolution kernels are sensitive to rotation, which motivates the hexagonal design studied here.

Method. HexaNet resamples each input image onto a hexagonal grid and applies hexagonal convolution kernels with six equidistant neighbours. The network has twelve layers and uses batch normalization and the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001. Datasets. We evaluate on EuroSAT, which contains 27000 labeled Sentinel-2 images in ten classes, and on a private collection of 4000 aerial tiles. Results. On EuroSAT, HexaNet reaches an accuracy of 96.4%, compared with 94.1% for ResNet-18. The model has 3.2 million parameters, which is 70% fewer than ResNet-18.

Limitations. HexaNet requires a resampling step that increases preprocessing time by roughly 40%. The method was tested only on optical imagery and may not transfer to radar data. Training used a single random seed, so variance across runs is unknown. Conclusion. Hexagonal kernels improve rotation robustness and accuracy at a lower parameter count. Future work. We plan to evaluate multispectral inputs and to study hexagonal pooling layers.

documents.title: DepthRAG: Adaptive Retrieval Depth for Open-Domain Question Answering
pages: DepthRAG: Adaptive Retrieval Depth for Open-Domain Question Answering. SYNTHETIC TEST FIXTURE - fictional content written for software testing; not a real publication. Abstract. We propose DepthRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation system that chooses how many passages to retrieve for each question. The objective is to reduce generation cost without lowering answer quality. Problem statement. Fixed retrieval depth wastes tokens on easy questions and under-retrieves for multi-hop questions.

Method. DepthRAG uses a small classifier built on a BERT encoder to predict question complexity and then sets the retrieval depth between 2 and 12 passages. Retrieval combines BM25 with dense retrieval, and a cross-encoder reranks the candidates. Datasets. Experiments use Natural Questions and HotpotQA. Results. On Natural Questions, DepthRAG attains an exact match of 41.8, versus 40.9 for a fixed depth of 8 passages, while using 35% fewer prompt tokens. On HotpotQA the exact match is 33.2.

Limitations. The complexity classifier was trained only on English questions. Latency measurements exclude the classifier warm-up. Gains on HotpotQA were within one standard deviation. Conclusion. Adaptive depth lowers cost with comparable accuracy. Future work. We intend to test multilingual questions and to learn the depth policy end to end.

documents.title: PhishGraph: Graph Neural Networks for Phishing URL Detection
pages: PhishGraph: Graph Neural Networks for Phishing URL Detection. SYNTHETIC TEST FIXTURE - fictional content written for software testing; not a real publication. Abstract. We present PhishGraph, a graph neural network that detects phishing websites by modelling links between domains. The objective is to detect phishing URLs that evade lexical filters. Problem statement. Attackers rotate domains quickly, so detectors based only on URL strings miss newly registered domains.

Method. PhishGraph builds a graph whose nodes are domains and whose edges are hyperlinks and shared hosting records, and applies a two-layer graph convolutional network (GCN). Datasets. We use a crawl of 120000 domains labeled from public blocklists. Results. PhishGraph achieves an F1-score of 0.953 and a recall of 0.947, whereas a random forest on lexical features reaches an F1-score of 0.902.

Limitations. Labels come from blocklists, which lag behind new attacks and may contain errors. The crawl covers a single month, so concept drift is not measured. Graph construction is expensive for large crawls. Conclusion. Link structure gives a strong signal for phishing detection. Future work. We will study temporal graphs and adversarial attacks on the graph structure.
